projects.name: RideShare API v2
projects.description: A ride-sharing backend connecting drivers and passengers, built with FastAPI, async SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL. JWT auth, a server-side capability policy and row-level locking keep permissions and seat counts correct under concurrent requests.

image.alt: RideShare v2 React frontend landing page, served with the FastAPI API from one origin

highlights: Ride, then booking row locks (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) serialize accept, cancel and complete
Unique partial index blocks duplicate active bookings and maps to HTTP 409
One account acts as passenger and driver; permissions are checked on the server, never trusted from the client
v2 (rideshare-v2 branch): 194 tests passing in CI against real PostgreSQL, including concurrency and migration tests
projects.problem: Drivers publish rides with a fixed number of seats and passengers request them. Two concurrent accept or cancel requests can oversell seats, and a dashboard mode chosen in the browser must never be treated as permission.
projects.architecture: Routers declare the HTTP contract and services own the business rules and transactions on the request's AsyncSession. Every booking decision locks the Ride row first and then its bookings in ID order, so accept, cancel and complete serialize and seat changes commit atomically. A unique partial index on active bookings prevents duplicates. One ordinary account can act as passenger and driver: permissions.py is the shared server-side capability policy, and the frontend's selected mode is presentation only. Alembic owns the schema, and auth rate limiting is Redis-backed and opt-in. The v2 work lives on the rideshare-v2 branch, with a preview deployment on FastAPI Cloud serving the React frontend and the API from one origin.
projects.whatILearned: Correctness under concurrency comes from lock order and database constraints, not from checks in Python. PostgreSQL integration tests, including concurrency and migration upgrade/downgrade tests running in CI, made larger refactors safe.
projects.users: A ride-sharing backend connecting drivers and passengers. Drivers publish rides with a fixed number of seats; passengers search and request seats; drivers accept or decline requests and complete or cancel rides.
projects.role: Solo developer and maintainer: API design, data model and Alembic migrations, service layer, tests, CI and deployment. The React frontend lives in the same repository and is served by the API.
features: Registration and JWT login; GET /me returns the account and its allowed modes
Publish rides; search by origin, destination, departure window and minimum seats, with limit/offset pagination
Request a seat; drivers accept or decline; passengers cancel; drivers complete or cancel rides
Passenger view of my bookings, driver view of my rides and each ride's bookings
React 19 + Vite frontend served from the same origin as the API

decisions.title: Lock the ride, then its bookings
decisions.body: Every booking decision runs SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the Ride row first and then on its bookings in ID order. Accept, cancel and complete on the same ride serialize, and seat changes commit atomically, so two concurrent accepts cannot consume the same seat.

decisions.title: Let PostgreSQL enforce one active booking
decisions.body: A unique partial index on (ride_id, passenger_id) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'accepted') blocks duplicates even if two requests pass the application check at once. Only a violation of that named constraint is mapped to 409; other integrity errors are not misclassified.

decisions.title: Capabilities on the server, modes in the UI
decisions.body: One ordinary account gets both passenger and driver capabilities, and admin gets neither; public registration rejects admin. permissions.py is the shared policy every service checks. The dashboard mode chosen in the frontend is presentation only.

decisions.title: Alembic owns the schema
decisions.body: Four revisions define the schema, and application startup only checks database connectivity; it never calls create_all. CI runs a fresh upgrade before the suite, and migration tests cover upgrade, downgrade and re-upgrade.

security: JWT via python-jose (HS256/384/512) with an enforced minimum key length; decoding requires the expected claims
bcrypt (12 rounds) runs in a threadpool so hashing does not block the event loop
Startup rejects a missing, placeholder or short SECRET_KEY
Validation errors are sanitized so passwords and emails are not echoed back
Generic login and registration-conflict messages; GET /me omits CNIC and phone
Optional Redis rate limiter for auth: fixed windows, atomic Lua, HMAC-keyed, fails closed

testing.summary: v2 (rideshare-v2 branch): 194 tests passing in CI. The backend suite uses unittest against a real PostgreSQL 15 database, with Redis 7.4 as a service, after a fresh Alembic upgrade.
items: Concurrency races: accept vs cancel, and two concurrent accepts consuming one seat
bcrypt offload keeps the event loop responsive
testing.ciLabel: CI run on rideshare-v2: Ran 194 tests … OK (Oct 20, 2026)

deployment: v1 (main branch) was deployed on AWS EC2 behind Nginx, per its README; v2 (rideshare-v2 branch) runs on FastAPI Cloud, serving the React frontend and the API from one origin
Multi-stage Dockerfile: Node 22 builds the frontend, then a Python 3.11-slim image runs uvicorn on $PORT
Docker Compose runs PostgreSQL 15 for local development
GitHub Actions runs the PostgreSQL integration suite on pushes to main and rideshare-v2 and on every pull request
limits: Fixed-window rate limiting allows bursts, and the limiter stays disabled in production until the FastAPI Cloud ingress is verified
Offset pagination can shift under concurrent writes and returns no total count
A cancelled ride's seat count is bookkeeping, not real capacity
No driver verification is implemented or claimed
The JWT is kept in memory, so a page reload means signing in again
Frontend Vitest and Playwright tests exist but do not run in CI yet

projects.name: Gemma 4 Coding Agent
projects.description: My entry in Kaggle's Gemma 4 coding-agent competition: an autonomous agent built on Gemma 4 31B and Google's Agent Development Kit that works through Python coding tasks without human input.
highlights: Agent built with Google ADK on Gemma 4 31B
Runs within the free weekly Kaggle GPU quota
Main track: best public leaderboard score 0.20 (submission S006), up from 0.06 on the first of six submissions
Paper track: submitted a write-up, "When Thinking Helps—and Hurts", on October 28, 2026
projects.problem: An open-weight model has to fix real code inside strict GPU and time limits, with no human in the loop.
projects.architecture: This is a high-level summary while the competition is running. The agent is built with Google ADK on Gemma 4 31B and runs in Kaggle notebooks within the free weekly GPU quota. Every experiment is logged and compared before anything is submitted, including bounded reasoning budgets. Along the way I found a hang in the evaluation harness, where a synchronous command tool blocked the event loop, and tested a stricter command timeout as a safety change. Main track: six official submissions so far; the best public score is 0.20 (S006), up from 0.06 on the first.
projects.whatILearned: Local scores did not predict the leaderboard. Measuring on the official scorer early, and changing one variable at a time, saves scarce GPU hours.
limits: The public leaderboard covers about half of the test data and moves by roughly ±0.05 between draws, so 0.20 is a noisy estimate
Code, prompts and detailed results stay private until the competition rules allow publication after December 2, 2026; the paper-track write-up becomes public when the hackathon closes

projects.name: HireLoop AI
projects.description: An AI career workspace that analyses a resume, scores it against a job post, drafts tailored applications, tracks applications on a Kanban board and offers AI coaching with Google Gemini. Built using Bolt.new and Supabase, with AI-assisted code generation.

image.alt: HireLoop AI landing page showing the AI career workspace

highlights: Resume analysis, job matching, tailored drafts, Kanban tracker, analytics and AI coaching
Gemini runs in a Supabase Edge Function that requires a signed-in user
JSON response schemas and user-safe errors
Submitted to Bolt Builders Week 2026 on October 20, 2026
projects.problem: Job seekers juggle resumes, job posts, drafts and follow-ups across tabs, and general-purpose AI tools readily invent experience that is not on the resume.
projects.architecture: A React and TypeScript frontend on Supabase Auth and Postgres with row-level security. Gemini calls run in a Supabase Edge Function that requires an authenticated user, uses JSON response schemas and returns user-safe errors. Resumes upload as PDF, DOCX or TXT and are parsed in the browser. A code check rejects drafts that claim employment at the target company, with one retry.
projects.whatILearned: Shipping an LLM feature means owning its failure modes. Gemini's thinking tokens were silently truncating JSON output; the fix disabled thinking for these calls and enforced JSON response schemas. Prompts alone do not stop invented claims, so the riskiest one also gets a code check.
projects.kind: Personal product · built with Bolt + Supabase
projects.role: Product requirements and MVP scope, testing live builds, release approvals and the Bolt Builders Week submission. Built using Bolt.new and Supabase, with AI-assisted code generation.
limits: Job Match scores and drafts live only in page state and are lost on reload
The no-invented-experience rule is mostly prompt-enforced; only the employment-at-target-company claim has a code check
The code lives in Bolt.new and Supabase, so there is no public repository

additionalProjects.name: AI Python Repair API
additionalProjects.label: Prototype (2026)
additionalProjects.description: A FastAPI service where Google Gemini proposes a fix for a Python file, ast.parse validates the syntax, and an invalid fix is retried up to 3 times.
additionalProjects.note: Early prototype; no test suite yet. Not safe to expose publicly: its /fix endpoint reads and overwrites client-supplied server file paths and has no authentication (documented in the README). An earlier demo on AWS EC2 behind Nginx is no longer online.
